newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ Maori TV property lease questioned by lessor.
newsitem.headline: NZ Maori TV property lease questioned by lessor.

text.p: The lease on Aotearoa Television Network's building may have been assigned without the required approval of the lessor, a director of property company Terra Firma said on Friday.
The director, Martin Lekner, told Reuters in a telephone interview that a client of Terra Firma had the lease on the Auckland building and it was sub-leased to 601 Digital Ltd.

The Independent Business Weekly reported a company asssociated with Aotearoa director Derek Burns bought the assets of 601 Digital for $813,000 and on-sold them soon after for $2.3 million to Maori television station Aotearoa. It is not clear whether the lease was part of those transactions.
Property industry sources told Reuters the property was leased to 601 Digital for about $300,000 a year for four years in December.

"We don't know (if it is subleased). We wrote to 601 in January because we became aware of at least one of the parties selling his interest. We have just asked them. It may now be a sub-sub-lease," Lekner said.

"If there is a substantive change in shareholding and the entire company is sold then a normal district law society lease calls for a lessor's approval and that step hasn't been advanced yet as far as I am aware. But it is pending.
"We haven't even been asked for it (our approval) so we haven't even got out of the blocks," he said.
He said Aotearoa would have common law rights and a change of ownership was not as draconian a breach of the lease as refusing to pay rent or making major physical changes.
Lekner said he did not know the terms of any sub-sub- leasing.
"All we are concerned about is the rental we have contracted to receive. That we get that."
He said if the building had been "sub-sub-leased" to Aotearoa Television he would be surprised if the price was higher than the original Terra Firma sub-lease.

"It was a heavy negotiation on that - it is definitely a market rental. It was not -- what was (Deputy Prime Minister Winston) Peters saying last night? - a realty rort. It is an absolutely standard sort of lease with a term of four years from December 1996."

Asked if he thought the lease would be increased in value as it was passed on to Aotearoa, Lekner said: "I don't think leases ever value up unless they are proven to be heavily concessionary and fixed for a term with no rent review. This is a normal lease so I doubt that is the case.

"Frankly I think the lease would be neutral in that (transaction). There is no concessionary aspect of it to value. It was a market negotiation with real estate people involved and it was negotiated quite vigorously."

New Zealand's Serious Fraud Office said on Thursday it had launched a preliminary inquiry into the Aotearoa Television Network and there are other investigations by Commerce Ministry officials and private contacts of Deputy Prime Minister Winston Peters.
On Friday Labour MP Trevor Mallard and Act New Zealand MP Derek Quigley examined Aotearoa's books.

After the examination Mallard said it appeared someone had made at least $1 million out of the channel, but he did not know to what extent that involved taxpayer money until after an examination of more detailed financial documents.

Peters initiated his inquiries after revelations of links between the company and two men at the centre of the "Winebox" tax inquiry into use of the Cook Islands as a tax haven by New Zealand corporates in the 1980s.
On Monday cabinet agreed to provide $4 million to keep the television network on air until June. The company produces Maori language television programmes for an Auckland audience.
